isable for every configured MCP server
# dsh-mcp-mcp-status
An installable DeepSeek Harness plugin that adds an **MCP** section to the Web Settings dialog, list
ing every MCP server the active profile configures with its derived status, transport, target, regis
tered tools, and an enable/disable switch.
The package replaces the MCP inventory earlier DSH releases shipped in-tree (`@deepseek-ai/dsh-host-
mcp-inventory` and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-ui-settings-mcp`) as one dual-face package: the package
root is the Host side (`mcpInventory` service) and the `./client` export is the browser side (the Se
ttings section). It reads only published surfaces — the Loader and the tool registry — so no DSH rel
ease has to carry an inventory-publication seam for it to work.
## What it does
The Settings section lists one row per configured MCP server: the server name from the entry's confi
g (falling back to the Loader entry id), a status tag, the transport and connection target from that
stored config, the tools registered under the server's namespace, and a switch. Its navigation row
draws the package's own glyph — a server node above two tool nodes — through the shell's `settings.s
ection.icon` slot instead of the shell's fallback icon.
The status is derived from the Loader entry and the tool registry: `disabled` for a row the profile
has switched off, which is still listed because the configured set comes from the Loader rather than
from a connection; `failed` when the entry's Loader fiber is in its failed phase; `connected` once
the server has registered at least one tool under its `mcp__<serverName>__` namespace; and `starting
` in every remaining case.
Two situations are indistinguishable in that derivation: a server that is negotiating or retrying re
ports `starting`, exactly like one that has not started yet, and a connected server that registers n
o tool reports `starting` as well. The text of the last connection failure is not exposed by any of
these surfaces, so the section no longer renders it.
The switch persists one server's enablement in the current profile through the profile manager and r
eturns the re-read inventory; when the Host has no profile manager composed, `managementAvailable` i
s false and the section renders the switches inert rather than pretending the write would work.
Nothing here is model-visible: the Host service reads the Loader configuration and the tool registry
, and the section reads that service. No prompt, tool schema, or session log entry is involved.
## Install from a git checkout
Substitute your GitHub owner for `<user>`; the repository must be named `dsh-mcp-mcp-status` so the
installed package name matches the profile's dependency key (rename the repository and pnpm derives
a different key, which then needs an alias such as `dsh-mcp-mcp-status@github:<user>/other-name`).

## Compatibility
The Host half imports only published surfaces: `@deepseek-ai/cordis-plugin-loader` for the Loader en
tries, `@deepseek-ai/dsh-tools` for the tool registry, and `@deepseek-ai/dsh-typert-protocol` for th
e Remote decorators. No DSH release has to export a publication seam for it, and `tsc -b tsconfig.ho
st.json` compiles the half against the published `0.2.0-rc.2`.
The consequence is concrete: with the seam gone, nothing in the build or at runtime waits for a rele
ase that carries one, and the published `0.2.0-rc.2` packages satisfy every import this package make
s — the Loader's entry list and fiber state and the registry's `schemas()` are public members of the
published surfaces.
Every `@deepseek-ai/dsh-*` dependency and peer is `^0.2.0-rc.2`; `@deepseek-ai/cordis` is `~4.0.4` a
nd `@deepseek-ai/cordis-plugin-loader` is `~1.0.5`, both being published on their own version lines
rather than the DSH line.
## Known limitations
The ported unit tests are not included. They were written against `@deepseek-ai/dsh-client-test-runt
ime`, which is not published, so the browser suites cannot resolve their runtime; `vitest` and `@tes
ting-library/react` would add a test-only dependency tree to a package whose whole job is a build-ti
react` would add a test-only dependency tree to a package whose whole job is a build-time `prepare`.
The browser baseline in `tsdown.client.ts` is a copy of the shell's static module table (`PLATFORM_M
ODULES` plus the empty `PRELOADED_CLIENT_EXTERNALS`). A row added to the shell's table after this fi
le was written is not requested by this package, so it would be inlined here instead of shared; that
is a duplicated module identity, not a load failure, and it is fixed by adding the specifier to the
duplicated module identity, not a load failure, and it is fixed by adding the specifier to the copy.
No run against a live profile was possible in the port environment: no `dsh web` observation covers
the row, the patch layering, the namespace reuse, or the Settings rendering, so those are documented
from the source they were ported from. The build does complete with a Typert generator that recogni
zes installed package owners: the Host bundle emits `packages/status/lib/typert.host.*` and `package
s/status/lib/typert.remote-client.*`, and both `tsc -b tsconfig.host.json` and `tsc -b tsconfig.clie
nt.json` exit 0. Without that recognition the generator fails the Host bundle step with `typert(host
): dsh-mcp-mcp-status publishes Remote artifacts but has no Remote methods`, and the browser half th
en cannot resolve the `dsh-mcp-mcp-status/remote` artifact that step emits. Building this package fr
om npm alone therefore waits on a `@deepseek-ai/dsh-typert-generator` release carrying that recognit
pm alone therefore waits on a `@deepseek-ai/dsh-typert-generator` release carrying that recognition.
`README.i18n.yaml` is intentionally absent. The bilingual pairing record next to a translated README
is generated by the harness repository's own `verify-translation-pairing --write` step, which does
not exist in this standalone repository; hand-writing its per-heading digests would record values no
is standalone repository; hand-writing its per-heading digests would record values nothing verified.
